pos: n. (a fragrant unguent, especially the holy anointing oil; rendering Hebrew shemen, merqachath, Greek muron)
etymology: From Latin unguentum, from unguere, to anoint — the same root as unction. In Scripture ointment is rarely cosmetic; it is consecration made visible.
biblical_def: Ointment in the Authorized Version is chiefly a holy thing. Exodus prescribes it exactly: “thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil” (Exo 30:25) — a specific compound, forbidden for common use, by which priests and kings were set apart. Psalm 133 makes it the emblem of unity: “It is like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard” (Psa 133:2) — brotherly concord pictured as consecrating oil running down, always downward, from the head to the skirts. Proverbs takes it into friendship: “Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel” (Pro 27:9). And Ecclesiastes weighs it against a life: “A good name is better than precious ointment” (Ecc 7:1). Every strand converges on the woman at Bethany, who broke an alabaster box of very precious ointment over the Anointed One Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ointment as any soft unctuous substance used for smearing, particularly the body or a diseased part — and notes the Scriptural use of the holy ointment for consecration.
webster_full: OINT´MENT, n. Unguent; any soft unctuous substance or compound, used for smearing, particularly the body or a diseased part.
2. In Scripture, the holy ointment, a compound of oil and spices, used in consecrating the priests and the vessels of the sanctuary.
Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savor. Eccles. x.
scriptures: And thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil.
It is like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard: that went down to the skirts of his garments;
Pro 27:9
Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel.
Ecc 7:1
A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth.
corruption_summary: Anointing detached from office and appropriated as a private spiritual sensation — men claiming an anointing for themselves — where Scripture makes it a consecration conferred, poured on from above and running downward.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern charismatic usage speaks of a man having an anointing, a portable quality of power attaching to a personality and often to a platform. Exodus 30 makes anointing something done to a person by appointment, with a compound God specified and expressly forbade for common use. The direction matters as much as the substance: in Psalm 133 the ointment runs down — head to beard to the skirts of the garments — and never up. Consecration descends. It is not generated by the one anointed.

The recovery is in the New Testament's own use of the figure. The anointing believers have is from the Holy One and abides in them, and it belongs to the whole body rather than to a class of specialists. That reading restores Psalm 133's point exactly, since the oil on Aaron's head was for the sake of the congregation he represented. And Ecclesiastes 7:1 keeps the whole subject honest: a good name outranks the most precious ointment. Character outlasts unction.
roots_summary: Hebrew shemen (H8081), oil, fatness; merqachath (H4842), a compounded unguent; mashach (H4886), to anoint — the root of Messiah; Greek muron (G3464), fragrant ointment.
roots_lines: Hebrew shemen (H8081) — oil, ointment, fatness; the precious ointment on Aaron's head (Psa 133:2).
Hebrew mashach (H4886) — to smear, anoint; from it mashiach, Messiah, the Anointed One — so this entry runs straight to Christ.
Greek muron (G3464) — ointment, perfume; the alabaster box broken over the Lord at Bethany (Mar 14:3).
usage: “An oil of holy ointment… it shall be an holy anointing oil” — a compound God specified.
“Like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down” — consecration always descends.
“A good name is better than precious ointment” — character outlasts unction.

pos: n. (a stool for the feet; in Scripture, the earth, the ark, and the place of subdued enemies; rendering Hebrew hadom, Greek hupopodion)
etymology: A plain English compound. Scripture makes it one of its largest images: what is beneath the feet of a seated King.
biblical_def: Footstool is a throne-word. Because a king sits and rests his feet, whatever is his footstool is both near him and under him — and Scripture assigns three things to that position. The earth itself: “The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me?” (Isa 66:1), which permanently forbids any theology that houses God in a building. The ark and the sanctuary: David calls the ark “the footstool of our God” (1Ch 28:2), and the Psalter summons the congregation to “worship at his footstool; for he is holy” (Psa 99:5) — worship is offered at the feet, never at the level of the throne. And His enemies: “Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool” (Psa 110:1), the most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament, and the Bible's definitive statement of the reign of Christ between the ascension and the end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a footstool simply as a stool for the feet, that on which the feet rest when sitting — and notes the Scriptural use for the earth and for subdued enemies.
webster_full: FOOT´STOOL, n. A stool for the feet; that which supports the feet of one when sitting.
The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. Is. lxvi.
Until I make thine enemies thy footstool. Ps. cx.
scriptures: A Psalm of David. The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
Isa 66:1
Thus saith the LORD, The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest?
Psa 99:5
Exalt ye the LORD our God, and worship at his footstool; for he is holy.

Then David the king stood up upon his feet, and said, Hear me, my brethren, and my people: As for me, I had in mine heart to build an house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and for the footstool of our God, and had made ready for the building:
corruption_summary: An over-realized triumphalism that treats the enemies as already underfoot, and an under-realized despair that doubts they ever will be — both misread the single word until.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The errors here are internal to the church and both turn on Psalm 110:1. One party reads the subjugation as finished and expects a Christendom without opposition, and is scandalized by every setback. The other reads the delay as doubt and expects only defeat until the end. The verse holds a precise middle: Christ is already seated at the right hand, which is the language of accomplished authority, and the enemies are being made His footstool, which is the language of a process with a term. He reigns now; the subduing is under way.

Isaiah 66:1 supplies the principle to recover for worship. If the earth is merely God's footstool, then no building contains Him and no institution manages Him, and the question where is the house that ye build unto me? is aimed at religious presumption in every age. Psalm 99:5 then shows the only fitting posture: worship at the footstool, low, on the ground — and the reason given is not sentiment but holiness.
roots_summary: Hebrew hadom (H1916), a footstool — used only with raglayim, feet; Greek hupopodion (G5286), literally under-foot-thing, the word in every New Testament citation of Psalm 110.
roots_lines: Hebrew hadom (H1916) — footstool; applied to the ark (1Ch 28:2), the sanctuary (Psa 132:7), and the earth (Isa 66:1).
Greek hupopodion (G5286) — a footstool, that under the feet; Heb 1:13 and Heb 10:13 press the until of Psa 110:1.
Hebrew hadom raglai — the footstool of my feet; the full idiom, emphasizing nearness as well as subjection.
usage: “Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool” — seated now, subduing still.
“The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool” — no building contains Him.
“Worship at his footstool; for he is holy” — the posture is low, and the reason is holiness.

pos: n. (a burning ember; rendering Hebrew gachelet, retseph, Greek anthrax)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon col. In Scripture a coal is almost always live — a burning ember taken from an altar or a hearth, never inert fuel.
biblical_def: Coal in the Authorized Version means a live ember, and it is nearly always taken from a fire that is already burning to God. On the Day of Atonement the high priest takes “a censer full of burning coals of fire from off the altar before the LORD” and carries them within the vail (Lev 16:12) — the incense of intercession must be kindled by altar fire, not by any fire of a man's own. Isaiah's cleansing follows the same rule: a seraph takes a live coal from the altar and touches his unclean lips. The Psalter uses coals for theophany — “coals were kindled by it” (Psa 18:8), “hail stones and coals of fire” (Psa 18:12) — and Elijah, at the end of himself under the juniper, is fed a cake baken on the coals (1Ki 19:6): the same element that pictures wrath also bakes bread for an exhausted prophet. Paul then makes coals an instrument of love: “thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head” by feeding an enemy (Rom 12:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines coal as a piece of wood or other combustible substance ignited and burning, or charred and extinguished — noting the Scriptural use of live coals from the altar.
webster_full: COAL, n. A piece of wood, or other combustible substance, ignited, burning, or charred.
2. In the plural, coals, embers; live coals.
3. A solid, opake, inflammable substance found in the earth, and dug from mines.
To heap coals of fire on the head, to excite by kindness the pangs of remorse in an enemy.
scriptures: And he shall take a censer full of burning coals of fire from off the altar before the LORD, and his hands full of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the vail:
At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hail stones and coals of fire.
And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again.
Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.
corruption_summary: Strange fire — worship kindled from a source God did not appoint — presented as zeal, while Romans 12:20 is read as a permission to wound rather than a command to feed.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 16:12 specifies where the coals come from: off the altar before the LORD. Nadab and Abihu died for offering incense with fire God had not commanded, and the principle governs worship still. Zeal, sincerity, and heat are not sufficient; the fire must be taken from the altar of atonement, which is to say that acceptable worship is kindled by the finished sacrifice and by nothing else. Every innovation that generates its own heat — emotional, aesthetic, or theatrical — is offering strange fire, however sincerely.

Romans 12:20 is often quoted with a smirk, as though heaping coals meant a superior form of revenge. Read the command it is attached to: if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink. The coals are the burning of shame that leads to repentance, and the instrument is a meal. Webster's definition catches it exactly — to excite by kindness the pangs of remorse. A Christian who uses the verse to justify hostility has inverted the only sentence it appears in.
roots_summary: Hebrew gachelet (H1513), a live coal, burning ember; ritspah (H7531), a hot stone or coal — the seraph's coal in Isa 6:6; Greek anthrax (G440), a burning coal.
roots_lines: Hebrew gachelet (H1513) — a live coal; the censer of coals from the altar on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:12).
Hebrew ritspah (H7531) — a live coal or hot stone; taken with tongs from the altar to touch Isaiah's lips (Isa 6:6).
Greek anthrax (G440) — a burning coal; Paul's coals of fire heaped by feeding an enemy (Rom 12:20).
usage: “A censer full of burning coals of fire from off the altar” — incense kindled by altar fire only.
“A cake baken on the coals” — the same element bakes bread for a spent prophet.
“Thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head” — and the instrument is a meal.

pos: n. (the ordered art of sound; the Authorized Version's spelling of music; rendering Hebrew shir, zimrah, and instruments of shir)
etymology: From Greek mousike, the art of the Muses, through Latin musica. The 1611 spelling musick is preserved here because it is the form the Authorized Version uses throughout.
biblical_def: Musick in the Authorized Version is almost always instruments of musick, and almost always in the service of praise. David's great institution is the founding text: he “spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals” (1Ch 15:16) — appointed men, appointed instruments, appointed order. The high-water mark comes at the dedication of the temple, and the detail is worth weighing: when the trumpeters and singers “were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD… then the house was filled with a cloud” (2Ch 5:13). The glory falls on unity of sound, not on volume or virtuosity. Musick also serves ordinary joy — the women meet Saul with tabrets and instruments of musick (1Sa 18:6) — and Lamentations shows its cruellest use, when a suffering man becomes the song: “I am their musick” (Lam 3:63).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines music as a succession of sounds so modulated as to please the ear, and the science of harmonical sounds — noting its use in sacred worship among the Hebrews.
webster_full: MU´SIC, n. Melody or harmony; any succession of sounds so modulated as to please the ear, or any combination of simultaneous sounds in accordance or harmony.
2. The science of harmonical sounds, which treats of the principles of harmony.
3. Order; harmony in revolutions.
Music among the Hebrews was much used in their religious worship, and in their public rejoicings.
scriptures: And David spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals, sounding, by lifting up the voice with joy.

It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD; and when they lifted up their voice with the trumpets and cymbals and instruments of musick, and praised the LORD, saying, For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: that then the house was filled with a cloud, even the house of the LORD;

And it came to pass as they came, when David was returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, that the women came out of all cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet king Saul, with tabrets, with joy, and with instruments of musick.
Lam 3:63
Behold their sitting down, and their rising up; I am their musick.
corruption_summary: Church musick evaluated as performance and as emotional engineering — the congregation an audience, the sound a product — where 2 Chronicles 5:13 hangs everything on being as one.
corruption_paragraphs: The professionalizing of church musick has quietly reversed its direction. Where sound is produced for a congregation rather than by it, the people become an audience, and the measure of a service becomes how it made them feel — which is emotional engineering, whatever the lyrics say. 2 Chronicles 5:13 sets a different test: the glory descends when trumpeters and singers are as one, to make one sound. Unity, not excellence, is the stated condition, and the content of that one sound is named: for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever.

The Reformed reader will want the regulative principle applied here, and rightly — what God has commanded in worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. That is a live discussion regarding instruments, since the Levitical arrangement was appointed for a temple that has been fulfilled and torn down. What is not in dispute is the object and the order: appointed men, sung Scripture, and one sound offered to God rather than to the room. Lamentations 3:63 supplies the sober footnote — musick can also be a weapon, and a mocking song is still a song.
roots_summary: Hebrew shir (H7892), a song, and kley shir, instruments of song; zimrah (H2172), melody, psalmody; neginah (H5058), a stringed-instrument song — and also a taunting song.
roots_lines: Hebrew shir (H7892) — a song; kley shir, vessels or instruments of song, is the phrase behind instruments of musick (1Ch 15:16).
Hebrew zimrah (H2172) — melody, psalm; the root of the Psalter's own title-words and of mizmor, a psalm.
Hebrew neginah (H5058) — a stringed song; in Lam 3:63 it is a mocking song, the sufferer himself made the musick.
usage: “Singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals” — appointed men and order.
“As one, to make one sound… then the house was filled with a cloud” — unity is the condition.
“I am their musick” — a song can be a weapon.

pos: n. (a royal staff, the emblem of sovereign authority; rendering Hebrew shebet, sharbit, Greek rhabdos)
etymology: From Greek skeptron, a staff to lean on, through Latin sceptrum. The Hebrew shebet means both a rod of rule and a tribe — a people gathered under one staff.
biblical_def: Sceptre is the emblem of the right to rule, and Scripture makes it a messianic word from Genesis onward. Jacob's blessing on Judah is the hinge of Old Testament expectation: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be” (Gen 49:10). Balaam — a hired prophet who could not curse — sees the same thing: “there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel” (Num 24:17). The Psalter then addresses the King as God and describes His rule by its quality: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre” (Psa 45:6) — a verse Hebrews applies directly to the Son. Esther supplies the human picture that makes the doctrine felt: no one may approach the king uncalled and live, “except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre” (Est 4:11). Access is a gift of the sceptre, never a right of the petitioner.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sceptre as a staff or baton borne by kings on solemn occasions as a badge of authority, and hence as royal power or sovereignty itself.
webster_full: SCEP´TER, n. A staff or baton borne by kings on solemn occasions, as a badge of authority.
Hence, 2. The appropriate ensign of royalty; and figuratively, royal power or authority.
The sceptre shall not depart from Judah. Gen. xlix.
SCEP´TER, v.t. To invest with royal authority, or with the ensign of authority.
scriptures: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.
Psa 45:6
Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.

I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.
Est 4:11

All the king's servants, and the people of the king's provinces, do know, that whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days.
corruption_summary: The lordship of Christ reduced to a private preference — a sceptre over the inner life only — where Scripture makes it a public rule to which the gathering of the peoples belongs.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern settlement permits Christ a sceptre over the heart and the congregation and denies Him one anywhere else. But Genesis 49:10 says the gathering of the peoples is to Him, and Psalm 45:6 calls the sceptre of His kingdom a right sceptre — a standard of rule, not a private devotion. A confession that Jesus is Lord of the believer's feelings and of nothing outside them is not a smaller version of the biblical claim; it is a different claim.

Esther 4:11 is where the doctrine turns pastoral, and it is the passage to recover. In Persia, approaching the king uncalled was death unless he extended the golden sceptre. That is the natural position of every sinner before God, and it explains why access is always spoken of as a mercy. The believer comes boldly — but boldly because the sceptre has been extended in Christ, not because the throne room was ever open by right. Esther's if I perish, I perish is what approach costs without a mediator.
roots_summary: Hebrew shebet (H7626), a rod, staff, sceptre — and also a tribe; sharbit (H8275), the Persian golden sceptre of Esther; Greek rhabdos (G4464), a rod — the rod of iron in Revelation.
roots_lines: Hebrew shebet (H7626) — rod, staff, sceptre, and tribe; the sceptre that shall not depart from Judah (Gen 49:10).
Hebrew sharbit (H8275) — a sceptre; used only in Esther, of the golden sceptre held out to grant life (Est 4:11; Est 5:2).
Greek rhabdos (G4464) — a rod, staff, sceptre; Heb 1:8 applies Psa 45:6 to the Son, a sceptre of righteousness.
usage: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah… until Shiloh come” — the hinge of Old Testament expectation.
“The sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre” — a standard of rule, not a preference.
“Except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre” — access is a gift.

pos: n. (a bent piece of metal for hanging or catching; rendering Hebrew vav, chach, chakkah)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hoc. The Hebrew name of the tabernacle hook, vav, became the sixth letter of the alphabet — a letter shaped like the peg it is named for.
biblical_def: Hook is a small word with two very different offices. In the tabernacle it is a fastening: the vail hangs “upon four pillars of shittim wood overlaid with gold: their hooks shall be of gold” (Exo 26:32), and the court's pillars are “filleted with silver; their hooks shall be of silver” (Exo 27:17). The metals are graded by nearness to the holy place — gold within, silver in the court, brass at the sockets — and the hooks are what hold the whole hanging structure together. That the Hebrew word vav is also the letter and, the conjunction that joins, is a happy providence of language. The second office is capture: the LORD tells Sennacherib, “I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back” (2Ki 19:28) — an empire led home like an animal. Amos threatens the same for the luxurious women of Samaria (Amo 4:2). What fastens the sanctuary also fastens the tyrant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hook as a piece of iron or other metal bent into a curve for catching, holding and sustaining any thing — and notes the pruning-hook and the fishing-hook as distinct kinds.
webster_full: HOOK, n. A piece of iron or other metal bent into a curve for catching, holding and sustaining any thing; as a hook for hanging a pot.
2. A snare; a trap.
3. A curving instrument for cutting grass or grain; a sickle.
By hook and by crook, one way or other; by any means, direct or indirect.
scriptures: And thou shalt hang it upon four pillars of shittim wood overlaid with gold: their hooks shall be of gold, upon the four sockets of silver.
All the pillars round about the court shall be filleted with silver; their hooks shall be of silver, and their sockets of brass.
Because thy rage against me and thy tumult is come up into mine ears, therefore I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest.
Their pillars were twenty, and their brasen sockets twenty; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver.
corruption_summary: Small and unglamorous offices despised in the body of Christ — the fastenings nobody names — while the age also forgets that God rules tyrants by a hook they never see.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's doctrine of the members, illustrated here in metal. No one ever admired a tabernacle hook. It is invisible when the work is done, and the whole vail hangs from it. A congregation that honours only its visible offices has misread the tabernacle inventory, in which the Holy Ghost troubled to record the metal of every hook and fillet. God's accounting includes the fastenings.

The second recovery is political and deeply comforting. Sennacherib came against Jerusalem in overwhelming force, and the LORD's answer was not an army but an image: I will put my hook in thy nose. The empire imagined it was choosing its route; it was being led. That is the doctrine of providence over rulers in its most vivid form, and it is the reason a believer may read the news without terror. The hooks that hold the sanctuary together and the hook in the tyrant's nose are held in the same hand.
roots_summary: Hebrew vav (H2053), a peg or hook — also the sixth letter of the alphabet; chach (H2397), a ring or hook put in the nose; chakkah (H2443), a fish-hook.
roots_lines: Hebrew vav (H2053) — a hook, peg; used only of the tabernacle fastenings, and the name of the letter that means and (Exo 26:32).
Hebrew chach (H2397) — a ring, hook, clasp; the hook in Sennacherib's nose (2Ki 19:28) and in leviathan's jaw (Job 41:2).
Hebrew chakkah (H2443) — a fish-hook; Habakkuk's image of nations taken up with the angle (Hab 1:15).
usage: “Their hooks shall be of gold” — the metal graded by nearness to the holy place.
“Their hooks shall be of silver, and their sockets of brass” — God records the fastenings.
“I will put my hook in thy nose” — an empire led home like an animal.

pos: v. (to dissolve by heat; figuratively, to lose courage; rendering Hebrew masas, mug, Greek luo, teko)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon meltan. Scripture's commonest use is not metallurgical but military: hearts, not metals, are what melt in the Old Testament.
biblical_def: Melt in Scripture is chiefly what happens to courage. Moses' song at the sea predicts it — “all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away” (Exo 15:15) — and Rahab reports it fulfilled forty years later in one of the great confessions of the Old Testament: “as soon as we had heard these things, our hearts did melt… for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath” (Jos 2:11). The melting is contagious in both directions: at Ai “the hearts of the people melted, and became as water” (Jos 7:5), and Caleb recalls that the unbelieving spies “made the heart of the people melt” while he wholly followed the LORD (Jos 14:8). A report melts a nation, and the report is usually carried by men who were sent to encourage. The word finally turns cosmic in Peter: “the elements shall melt with fervent heat” (2Pe 3:10) — the created order itself proving less solid than it looks.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines melt as to dissolve, to make liquid by heat, and figuratively as to soften to love or tenderness, or to dishearten and deprive of courage.
webster_full: MELT, v.t. To dissolve; to make liquid; to liquefy; to reduce from a solid to a liquid or flowing state by heat.
2. To dissolve; to reduce to first principles.
3. To soften to love or tenderness.
MELT, v.i. To become liquid; to dissolve. 2. To be softened to love, pity, tenderness or sympathy. 3. To faint; to be discouraged.
scriptures: Jos 2:11

And as soon as we had heard these things, our hearts did melt, neither did there remain any more courage in any man, because of you: for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.
Then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed; the mighty men of Moab, trembling shall take hold upon them; all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away.
Jos 14:8
Nevertheless my brethren that went up with me made the heart of the people melt: but I wholly followed the LORD my God.

But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.
corruption_summary: Courage treated as a temperament some possess rather than a fruit of what a man believes about God — while the melting effect of an unbelieving report on a whole congregation goes unreckoned.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The neglected doctrine is the contagiousness of unbelief. Joshua 14:8 states it without softening: the spies made the heart of the people melt. Ten men with a discouraging report cost a nation forty years. That is a warning to everyone who speaks to God's people — in a pulpit, a small group, or a conversation after the service — because a melted heart is rarely melted by an enemy. It is melted by a brother with a bad report.

The principle to recover is that courage is a function of doctrine, not disposition. Rahab's heart melted at exactly the same news that hardened Jericho's king, and she reasoned from it to a confession — the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath — and then acted. The melting was the beginning of her faith. What a man's fear does to him depends entirely on what he believes about the God who caused it.
roots_summary: Hebrew masas (H4549), to dissolve, faint, melt away — used of hearts and of manna; mug (H4127), to soften, dissolve; Greek luo (G3089), to loose, dissolve, in 2Pe 3.
roots_lines: Hebrew masas (H4549) — to melt, dissolve, faint; the hearts of Canaan (Jos 2:11) and of Israel at Ai (Jos 7:5).
Hebrew mug (H4127) — to melt, soften; the inhabitants of Canaan melting away in Moses' song (Exo 15:15).
Greek teko (G5080) — to melt with heat; the elements melting at the day of the Lord (2Pe 3:12).
usage: “Our hearts did melt… for the LORD your God, he is God” — Rahab reasons from fear to faith.
“Made the heart of the people melt: but I wholly followed the LORD” — a bad report costs forty years.
“The elements shall melt with fervent heat” — creation is less solid than it looks.

pos: adj. and pp. (cut and shaped with a tool; rendering Hebrew gazith, chatsab)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon heawan, to cut. The theological weight of the word lies in a prohibition: the altar of God may not be built of hewn stone.
biblical_def: Hewn means cut and dressed by a tool, and Scripture attaches a startling law to it: “if thou wilt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stone: for if thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it” (Exo 20:25). The workmanship of man pollutes the place of atonement — a plain statement, at the very foundation of Israel's worship, that human contribution defiles rather than improves the means of approach to God. Hewn stone is permitted everywhere else: Josiah's repairs use it freely (2Ki 22:6), and Wisdom herself “hath hewn out her seven pillars” (Pro 9:1). Isaiah 9:10 records the proud boast of a people refusing correction — “The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones” — rebuilding better rather than repenting. And Isaiah 51:1 turns the word into a call to humility: “look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives hewn as the participle of hew — cut with an edged instrument, chopped, shaped by cutting — and notes hewn stone as stone dressed with a tool.
webster_full: HEWN, pp. of HEW. Cut with an edged instrument; chopped; hacked.
2. Felled; as timber hewn in the forest.
3. Shaped by cutting; formed; as hewn stone.
Thou shalt not build it of hewn stone. Ex. xx.
scriptures: And if thou wilt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stone: for if thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it.
Isa 51:1
Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged.
Isa 9:10
The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars.
Pro 9:1
Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars:
corruption_summary: The altar improved — approach to God dressed up by human workmanship — which Exodus 20:25 does not call a lesser offering but a polluted one.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 20:25 is one of the most counter-intuitive sentences in the law. A dressed stone is better in every way a mason could name: truer, stronger, more beautiful. And the moment the tool touches it, the altar is polluted. God is not against skill — the tabernacle is full of devised work and Wisdom hews her own pillars — but the place where blood is shed for sin must show no mark of human improvement. Every scheme that adds a human contribution to the ground of acceptance is lifting a tool on the altar, however fine the finish.

Isaiah 9:10 shows the reflex the law was guarding against. Judgment falls, and the response is not repentance but an upgrade: the bricks are down, we will build with hewn stones. Better materials, same defiance. Isaiah 51:1 supplies the corrective posture, and it is one the church regularly needs: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn. Remember the quarry. Whatever shape you have now was cut out of the same pit as everyone else's.
roots_summary: Hebrew gazith (H1496), hewn stone, cut work — the forbidden material for an altar; chatsab (H2672), to hew, dig, quarry — the verb of Isa 51:1.
roots_lines: Hebrew gazith (H1496) — hewn stone, ashlar; forbidden for the altar (Exo 20:25) and boasted of by the impenitent (Isa 9:10).
Hebrew chatsab (H2672) — to hew out, quarry; the rock whence the covenant people were hewn (Isa 51:1), and Wisdom's pillars (Pro 9:1).
Hebrew cherev (H2719) — a tool, sword; the very word for the mason's implement in Exo 20:25, tying the tool to the sword.
usage: “If thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it” — human workmanship defiles the altar.
“The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones” — better materials, same defiance.
“Look unto the rock whence ye are hewn” — remember the quarry.

pos: n. (a vessel for boiling or storing; rendering Hebrew sir, tsintseneth, Greek stamnos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon pott. In Scripture the humblest vessel in the house becomes a memorial, a test of holiness, and a figure for the nation itself.
biblical_def: Pot is a common vessel that Scripture repeatedly loads with meaning. It is a memorial: “Take a pot, and put an omer full of manna therein, and lay it up before the LORD, to be kept for your generations” (Exo 16:33) — a kitchen jar set before God so that later generations would see what wilderness bread looked like. It is a measure of holiness: an earthen vessel in which a sin offering was boiled must be broken, but “if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water” (Lev 6:28) — porous things absorb what they contain, and some vessels cannot be cleansed, only destroyed. It is the emblem of the slavery men grow nostalgic for: Israel remembers “the flesh pots” of Egypt and wishes itself back (Exo 16:3). And Zechariah closes the canon's story of the pot by promising that every pot in Jerusalem shall be holiness unto the LORD — the whole distinction between sacred and common vessels finally abolished upward.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pot as a vessel more deep than broad, used for holding liquors and other things — and notes its many kinds, from the flesh-pot to the vessel of the potter.
webster_full: POT, n. A vessel more deep than broad, made of earth, or iron or other metal, used for several domestic purposes.
2. A vessel of earth, or a cup, in which flowers are cultivated.
3. A measure of liquids; the quart of two pints.
To go to pot, to be destroyed, ruined, wasted or expended. A low phrase.
scriptures: And Moses said unto Aaron, Take a pot, and put an omer full of manna therein, and lay it up before the LORD, to be kept for your generations.
Lev 6:28
But the earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken: and if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water.
Exo 16:3

And the children of Israel said unto them, Would to God we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.
And the pots, and the shovels, and the basons: and all these vessels, which Hiram made to king Solomon for the house of the LORD, were of bright brass.
corruption_summary: The sacred and the ordinary severed, so that religion is confined to designated objects and hours — where Scripture moves in the opposite direction, making the cooking-pot holy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to correct is the sacred/secular split, which the pot refutes from both ends. A kitchen jar holds the manna before the LORD; the flesh pots of Egypt become the emblem of a heart that prefers slavery with meat to freedom with God; and a common cooking vessel is regulated by the law of the sin offering. Nothing in an Israelite household was outside the covenant, which is precisely what a modern believer forgets between Sunday and Monday.

Leviticus 6:28 rewards close reading. An earthen pot that has boiled a sin offering must be broken, because porous clay absorbs; a brasen one may be scoured and used again. The lesson is not that some sinners are disposable but that some vessels take in what passes through them. Habits, appetites, and company soak into a man, and there are things a person cannot merely rinse. The doctrine of mortification is written into the kitchen inventory.
roots_summary: Hebrew sir (H5518), a pot, caldron — the flesh pots of Egypt; tsintseneth (H6803), the jar that held the manna; Greek stamnos (G4713), the golden pot of Heb 9:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew sir (H5518) — a pot, caldron; the flesh pots of Egypt (Exo 16:3) and the boiling pot of Jeremiah's vision (Jer 1:13).
Hebrew tsintseneth (H6803) — a receptacle, jar; used once, of the pot of manna laid up before the LORD (Exo 16:33).
Greek stamnos (G4713) — a jar; Hebrews calls it the golden pot that had manna, kept in the ark (Heb 9:4).
usage: “Take a pot, and put an omer full of manna therein” — a kitchen jar set before God.
“The earthen vessel… shall be broken” — porous things absorb what they hold.
“When we sat by the flesh pots” — nostalgia for slavery, remembered by its meat.

pos: n. (a precious ornament or gem; rendering Hebrew keli, segullah, nezem)
etymology: From Old French joel, from Latin jocale, a plaything, from jocus, jest. Scripture takes a word for a trinket and makes it the name God gives His people.
biblical_def: Jewel runs a remarkable course through Scripture. It begins as a bride-price: Abraham's servant brings out “jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment, and gave them to Rebekah” (Gen 24:53) — the ornaments that identify a woman as chosen for a son she has not yet met. It becomes the wages of the exodus, as Israel spoils Egypt of jewels of silver and gold (Exo 11:2) — and then, tragically, that same gold is what the people bring to Aaron for a calf. It becomes an offering: the willing-hearted bring “all jewels of gold” for the tabernacle (Exo 35:22), and the captains of thousands bring wrought jewels “to make an atonement for our souls before the LORD” (Num 31:50). And it ends as God's own word for His people: “they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him” (Mal 3:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a jewel as an ornament of dress, usually one containing a precious stone, and by extension a person or thing of inestimable value.
webster_full: JEW´EL, n. An ornament of dress usually made of gold, silver or other precious metal, and often set with precious stones.
2. A precious stone.
3. A name of fondness; as, my jewel.
4. Figuratively, that which is of great value; a person or thing highly esteemed.
scriptures: Mal 3:17
And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him.
And the servant brought forth jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment, and gave them to Rebekah: he gave also to her brother and to her mother precious things.

And they came, both men and women, as many as were willing hearted, and brought bracelets, and earrings, and rings, and tablets, all jewels of gold: and every man that offered offered an offering of gold unto the LORD.

We have therefore brought an oblation for the LORD, what every man hath gotten, of jewels of gold, chains, and bracelets, rings, earrings, and tablets, to make an atonement for our souls before the LORD.
corruption_summary: Worth located in what a person owns or displays, so that jewels adorn the self — where Malachi reverses the whole transaction and makes the redeemed themselves the jewels God gathers.
corruption_paragraphs: Ornament as a proof of worth is an old temptation and a well-funded modern industry, and Scripture engages it without prudishness. Jewels are given to a bride, offered for a sanctuary, and brought as atonement money; the Bible has no quarrel with beauty or with gold. The quarrel is with direction. Aaron's calf was made of the very jewels Egypt had paid out, which is what happens when ornament stops being offered and starts being displayed — the same metal becomes an idol without changing composition.

Malachi 3:17 is the verse that resets the whole entry, and it is worth sitting with. God speaks of a day when He makes up His jewels — the picture is of a king going through his treasury, selecting what he will keep. The redeemed are not the ones wearing the jewels; they are the jewels, gathered, counted, and spared “as a man spareth his own son that serveth him.” A believer tempted to establish his worth by display should notice that he has already been appraised and set aside.
roots_summary: Hebrew keli (H3627), a vessel, article, ornament — the general word rendered jewels; segullah (H5459), a peculiar treasure — the word behind Malachi's jewels; nezem (H5141), a ring.
roots_lines: Hebrew keli (H3627) — an article, vessel, ornament; jewels of silver, and jewels of gold (Gen 24:53; Exo 11:2).
Hebrew segullah (H5459) — a peculiar treasure, personal property of a king; God's word for Israel (Exo 19:5) and for His jewels (Mal 3:17).
Hebrew nezem (H5141) — a nose-ring or earring; the jewels given to Rebekah, and the earrings surrendered for the calf (Exo 32:2).
usage: “In that day when I make up my jewels” — the redeemed are the jewels, not the wearers.
“Jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment” — the tokens of a chosen bride.
“To make an atonement for our souls before the LORD” — jewels brought, not worn.
